sections.body_en:
Ahead of the wedding, the bride needs to learn the fundamentals of the mitzva of simḥat ona (the mitzva of marital joy and intimacy) and the laws of purity, and it is good to learn them with the help of a madrikhat kallot (bridal instructor). As in every field, there are better instructors and less good ones. The sign of a good instructor is that she is well versed in the halakhot and knows how to explain them well, and she expands on explaining the mitzva of simḥat ona and its value (as explained in Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato, chapters 1-3), and from there proceeds to explain the laws of tum'a and tahara (impurity and purity), which are meant to direct, elevate and intensify love and joy. But a less good instructor turns things upside down; she does not base her instruction on the essence of the mitzva, which is the complete union, and she does not explain the halakhot well either.

Nearly all brides today customarily make use of hormonal pills to regulate the timing of the last veset (menstrual period) before the wedding, so that it falls at a time that allows the bride to become pure in time for the wedding, and yet falls at least three weeks before the wedding, so that immediately after the bride becomes impure from dam betulim (hymenal blood) and stops taking the pills, the next veset will arrive, and the period of impurity will be shortened. One should know that there are different pills, and each of them suits most women, while in some women it causes slight bleeding between cycles or low mood. Therefore, the bride should consult a doctor who is familiar with the subject early enough to be able to take the pills for two cycles before the wedding, so that if she sees that the pills do not suit her, the doctor can change the type of pill or its dosage, and the bride will arrive at her wedding pure and calm.

sections.title_en: Taking Care to Avoid a Ḥuppat Nidda
sections.body_en:
The bride must make every possible effort to arrive at the wedding when she is pure. For otherwise the joy of the wedding will be greatly harmed, and the groom and bride will have to observe all the laws of harḥakot (distancing measures) that we learned above (in chapter 3). This includes that they will be forbidden to touch hands and to pass an object from one to the other. However, at the time of the ḥuppa, in order to prevent embarrassment, the groom will be permitted to cover the bride with the veil, to place the ring on her finger, and to give her the cup of wine and the ketuba, while trying not to touch her. In addition, until the bride becomes pure, the prohibition of yiḥud (seclusion) applies to them, and they will have to sleep in separate rooms in their parents' home, or in another house where other people are present (as explained below, section 13). Likewise, after the ḥuppa they will be forbidden to be secluded in the "yiḥud room."1

In addition, some say that the marriage depends on the groom and bride being secluded in complete seclusion that is fit for the mitzva of ona (marital relations), and when the bride is not pure they are forbidden to be secluded, and consequently the marriage does not take effect (Rambam). However, since postponing the wedding would cause great losses and distress, the custom is to follow the opinion of most poskim, and the wedding is held even when the bride is not pure – a ḥuppat nidda (a wedding held while the bride is nidda, in a state of menstrual impurity).2

notes_en.en: Four reasons for permitting the giving of the ring at a ḥuppat nidda: 1) Since she has not yet been betrothed, their status is like that of other men and women, who are permitted to pass an object from hand to hand even if they might unintentionally touch each other (Or Zaru'a 1:341). 2) According to Rambam and Yere'im there is no prohibition against passing something from hand to hand except for wine, and in order to prevent embarrassment, in a rabbinic law one may rely on them. 3) Even according to the stringent opinions, in order to prevent very great embarrassment, it is permitted to transgress a rabbinic prohibition. 4) Since it is done in front of everyone and for a short time, there is no concern. This is the practical ruling of Be'er Heitev EH 61:8; Binyan Tziyon 139; Ikrei Ha-dat YD 21:4; Divrei Malkiel 5:206; Darkhei Tahara 10:17. Likewise, the groom may hand over the ketuba and give the wine to the bride, taking care not to touch her hand. When they go to the yiḥud room they should not hold hands (according to Shulḥan Shlomo 13:14 [?], if they are very embarrassed, the bride may wear gloves and in this way they may hold hands). According to the custom of those of Ashkenazic and Yemenite descent, who customarily lock the yiḥud room, at a ḥuppat nidda it is forbidden to lock it, and one must even tell one of the family members to come in midway without knocking, and in this way the couple will not be there in violation of the prohibition of yiḥud.

Ketubot 56a explains that the acquisition of marriage is effected by ḥibat ḥuppa (the intimacy of the ḥuppa), and Rav Ashi was uncertain whether only a ḥuppa that is fit for bi'a (union) effects acquisition, or whether the ḥuppa effects acquisition even when it is not fit for bi'a, as in a ḥuppat nidda. The matter remained in doubt. Rambam ruled (Hilkhot Ishut 10:2): "But if she was a nidda, even though she entered the ḥuppa and he was secluded with her, the marriage is not completed, and she is still like an arusa (a betrothed woman)." This is also the view of the Geonim and Rif. In contrast, the view of Rosh, Ran, Ritva and others is that even a ḥuppat nidda completes the marriage, because seclusion fit for the mitzva of ona is not indispensable. All that the Gemara was uncertain about is the tosefet ketuba (the additional ketuba sum), whether the groom grants it at a ḥuppat nidda. In practice, SA EH 61:2 writes: "It is proper that she not marry until she becomes pure." And Rema wrote: "Now the custom is not to be particular, and they do not wait. Nevertheless, it is good to inform the groom beforehand that she is a nidda." For according to Rabbeinu Peretz, the problem with a ḥuppat nidda is the concern of mekaḥ ta'ut (a transaction made in error) when the groom does not know of it. And according to Beit Shmuel 64:5, even Rambam would agree that if the groom was informed, the ḥuppa effects acquisition. Therefore, in a pressing situation, a ḥuppat nidda may be held (Taz EH 44:7; Rav Pe'alim vol. 2, YD 20).

sections.body_en:
Ahead of her wedding the bride must become pure from her veset blood, and also from the concern of dam ḥimud ("blood of desire"), as we will learn in the next section. To begin the process of purification she must perform the bedika (internal examination) of hefsek tahara (the examination establishing that bleeding has ceased) at least eight days before the wedding. After that, when the sun sets, she begins counting the shiv'a neki'im (seven clean days). During the shiv'a neki'im the bride should examine herself twice every day, once in the morning and once before sunset. If this is difficult for her, she may examine herself once each day. If she forgot and examined herself only twice during the seven days, she has fulfilled the obligation of the bedikot (as explained above, 4:8).

The bedikot of hefsek tahara and of the shiv'a neki'im are carried out with a white cloth called an ed bedika (examination cloth), and they are meant to verify that there is no bleeding from the uterus (above, 4:2). Ordinarily these bedikot must be performed deep within the vagina and "in the holes and crevices," that is, on all sides of the vagina (above, 4:3). However, because of the hymen, the bride cannot examine inside the vagina but only at its opening, without causing the slightest pain, so that no blood comes out from the hymen.

The seven days end exactly one week after the hefsek: if the hefsek tahara was performed toward the end of Tuesday, and she began the shiv'a neki'im on the night of Wednesday (Tuesday night), then the following week too the shiv'a neki'im will end at the end of Tuesday, and immediately after tzeit ha-kokhavim (nightfall) on Tuesday night she may perform tevila (immersion).3

notes_en.en: If she forgot to perform the hefsek tahara bedika, she begins counting shiv'a neki'im on the following day, and if the seventh day ends on the wedding night, she immerses on the seventh day, since in practice she will meet the groom only at night (see above, 5:9, n. 9). If she forgot by two days or more, they hold a ḥuppat nidda and she immerses at the end of the shiv'a neki'im. However, when this is especially difficult, a Torah scholar should be consulted, since some say that in a pressing situation, if the veset ended long before, one may rely on those who hold that hefsek tahara is not indispensable (above, ch. 4, end of n. 9, and on the view of Zikhron Yosef, above, ch. 4, n. 4), and on Rambam, who holds that an external wiping examination suffices, which the bride presumably performed (above, ch. 4, n. 4). See Taharat Ha-bayit vol. 1, 9:1.

sections.body_en:
The Sages instituted that when a bride agrees to marry, she counts shiv'a neki'im and immerses. For perhaps, out of the realization that she is about to marry and to unite with her groom in complete union, her heart will go out to him in desire, and out of her excitement dam ḥimud will come out of her uterus and she will become impure from it (Nidda 66a). And even if she examined herself and did not see blood, it is possible that a little blood came out and was lost in the natural moisture found in the vagina. The time at which there is concern for dam ḥimud is the time of agreeing to marry, for then the bride becomes clearly aware that she is about to marry. If the agreement to marry was given long before the wedding, the time when there is a chance that she will see dam ḥimud is when the final preparations begin, about two or three weeks before the wedding.

Even a woman who does not menstruate, such as an older woman who has stopped seeing menstrual blood, since she received a marriage proposal and agreed, may become excited and see dam ḥimud, and she must count shiv'a neki'im and immerse ahead of her wedding (Nidda 66a). And although most likely she did not see blood, since the Sages instituted that a bride counts shiv'a neki'im and immerses ahead of her wedding, she must recite a blessing over the tevila.

A bride who is able to become pure from her last veset a week or two before the wedding should preferably postpone the shiv'a neki'im so that she immerses a day or two before her wedding, and at most four days before the wedding. For some say that the closer the wedding date approaches, the greater the chance that she will become excited and dam ḥimud will come out, and it is therefore good for her to bring her purifying tevila close to the date of her wedding. In addition, it is good that even after her tevila she examines herself every day until her wedding day with an external wiping examination, to make sure that she has not begun to see blood due to desire.4

If the bride immersed and became pure ahead of the wedding, and a quarrel broke out and they called off the wedding, and then they again agreed to marry, she must again count shiv'a neki'im and immerse, lest at the time the marriage was decided anew she saw dam ḥimud (SA YD 192:3).

Likewise, when a man takes back his divorced wife, even if she is pregnant by him, she must count shiv'a neki'im and become pure from the concern of dam ḥimud (SA YD 192:5; Radbaz 3:423; Torat Ha-shelamim 9).

Even when elderly people marry, the bride must count shiv'a neki'im and become pure. But if it is clear that the groom's virility has already ceased, and the purpose of the marriage is companionship and help, she need not be concerned about dam ḥimud or count shiv'a neki'im.5

notes_en.en:
According to most Rishonim, the concern is that at the time the bride agrees to marry she may see dam ḥimud, and since dam ḥimud comes out in a moment and stops, she does not need to perform a hefsek tahara but only to count shiv'a neki'im. Moreover, according to Ravya, since only at the moment of agreement is there a concern that she will see dam ḥimud, if she paid attention at that time and did not feel anything, she is pure and does not need shiv'a neki'im. However, the other Rishonim hold that we do not rely on her sensation; rather, we are concerned that she became impure, and she must count shiv'a neki'im and become pure. Regarding the bedikot of the shiv'a neki'im, some say that by the letter of the law she need not examine during the shiv'a neki'im (Rashba and Meiri), and many hold that in order for them to count as clean days she must examine herself once during the shiv'a neki'im (Ra'avad, Ramban, Tur and SA YD 192:1; Rashba in practice). And some say she should examine every day, as with all shiv'a neki'im (Re'ah).
In contrast, some say that the concern of dam ḥimud is not only at the time of agreeing to marry; rather, from the time of agreeing to marry until the wedding there is a concern that she may see dam ḥimud, and the closer the time of the wedding, "the more her heart stirs and wonders, and we are constantly concerned that she may see blood out of desire" (Rosh, Nidda 10:4). Therefore, although she does not need a hefsek tahara, she must examine on every one of the shiv'a neki'im. Based on this reasoning, the custom became to place the shiv'a neki'im close to the wedding (Tosafot Yoma 18b, s.v. "ve-ha-amar"; Rashbam and Hagahot Maimoniyot). Rema (192:2) wrote that according to this custom, the be'ilat mitzva (the first marital union) should also not be more than four days after the tevila, and if more than four days have passed from the tevila to the be'ilat mitzva, she should examine herself every day, lest out of her desire she saw blood. End quote. According to Baḥ (192:4) and Ḥokhmat Adam 115:3, even if she immersed less than four days before the be'ilat mitzva, she must examine herself every day between the tevila and the union. However, all this is le-khatḥila (the preferred practice), but be-di'avad (after the fact), even if more than a week passed and she did not examine, she is pure (Shiyurei Berakha and Ḥavot Da'at).
In practice, I wrote that it is good for her to examine herself with an external bedika every day until the wedding, since according to those who hold that the concern is at the time of the marriage proposal, we are dealing with a small amount of dam ḥimud, but according to those who hold that the closer the wedding, the greater the excitement, it seems that the concern is that the excitement will cause the veset to come early, and for that an external wiping examination suffices. In addition, a virgin cannot in any case examine much more than an external wiping, and this is combined with the view of Rambam and those who agree with him that even during the shiv'a neki'im an external wiping suffices (above, ch. 4, n. 4), and with the view of most Rishonim that the concern of dam ḥimud exists only at the beginning. A woman who is accustomed to look at the tissue after wiping in the bathroom thereby fulfils an external bedika.
Regarding the basis of the law of dam ḥimud, it is related in Nidda 20b that R. Elazar and Rava knew how to smell blood and tell whether it came out due to desire or due to the veset. According to Ran, on this basis they knew to declare a woman pure, because dam ḥimud is pure, and only in the case of a bride did the Sages forbid it, lest nidda blood be drawn out along with it. According to Or Zaru'a, dam ḥimud is pure by Torah law and forbidden by rabbinic law. According to most Rishonim and Aḥaronim, dam ḥimud that came out with a sensation is impure by Torah law, and the Sages' knowledge merely expressed their expertise in blood (Rashba and Tosafot Ha-Rosh ad loc.; Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 5:1; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 183:2, and many others). But if the dam ḥimud came out without a sensation, the bride's obligation of tevila is rabbinic, and all the more so when she did not see blood at all, the obligation of tevila is rabbinic (Maggid Mishneh, Issurei Bi'a 11:10; Taz 192:1, and others).

The essence of dam ḥimud stems from the excitement ahead of the joy of marriage, which involves a permanent union and simḥat ona. This can be learned from the law of a bride whose match was arranged without her having seen the groom: she must count shiv'a neki'im and become pure from the concern of dam ḥimud, and if afterwards, a few days before the wedding, she sees the groom for the first time, she need not be concerned again about dam ḥimud, because the main concern of dam ḥimud is at the time of the decision on the union of marriage (Ḥatam Sofer YD 184; Beit Shlomo 40, and many others). Likewise, a woman whose husband returned from overseas after a long time does not need to observe shiv'a neki'im (Tiferet Le-Moshe on Taz 1; Shulḥan Gavoha 192:9).
Some say that when a couple who had a long relationship without proper halakhic marriage merited to return in teshuva, and afterwards were moved to marry properly with ḥuppa and kiddushin, then even if her periods have stopped, and even if she has become pure from her nidda status, she must become pure ahead of the marriage with a hefsek tahara, shiv'a neki'im and tevila (Taharat Ha-bayit 9:4). However, the halakha follows most poskim, that she does not need to immerse, for since they were in a steady relationship, no special desire is aroused ahead of the marriage (Ashrei Ha-ish 26:36; Shevet Ha-Kehati 6:317). (According to Ḥavot Da'at 192:1, since the main concern that dam ḥimud will come out is at the time of the request to marry and the agreement, if beforehand she places a tightly inserted wad (mokh daḥuk) in the vagina, and after she agrees she removes it and sees that there is no blood on it, she will not need to observe shiv'a neki'im. In cases of great need, such as older people who wish to marry within a few days, one may rely on him.)

sections.title_en: A Spiritual Reason for Not Meeting in the Week Before the Wedding
sections.body_en:
According to the rules of halakha and the safeguards that the Sages set in the laws of ketamim (bloodstains), the law should have been that only if the bride actually sees blood due to desire does she become impure, but if in practice she sees no blood other than her regular menstrual blood, she need not be concerned about additional blood of desire. However, the Sages were more stringent in this law, and were concerned that dam ḥimud may have come out and she did not see it because it was lost, and they therefore instituted that every bride must become pure from the concern of dam ḥimud. It seems that the Sages also had a spiritual reason: that every bride should purify herself, ahead of her wedding, from the period of wondering and searching, in which she had not yet merited to complete herself in a partnership and could only desire and long. And she should sanctify herself through shiv'a neki'im and tevila ahead of her union with her husband in love and joy. The counting of these days is like the counting of the seven weeks that Israel counted toward the giving of the Torah, which is considered the "wedding day" between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Knesset Yisrael (the Congregation of Israel).

Following on from this, in recent generations a fine custom has spread among Israel that the groom and bride do not meet during the week leading up to the wedding, and many also try not to speak on the phone. It seems that the halakhic basis for this is in the words of the Rishonim who hold that the closer the date of the wedding approaches while they still cannot marry, the more the concern of dam ḥimud may increase, and if they meet there is greater reason for this concern. The spiritual reason for the custom is that during this special week, out of longing and yearning for the joy of marriage, they purify themselves from the period in which they were lacking and could only desire and long, and they sanctify themselves ahead of their marriage in joy and love.6

notes_en.en:
This custom suits the spiritual preparations required ahead of the wedding. Admittedly, in the past this custom was less observed, since the families of the groom and bride often lived in different towns and arrived at the wedding a day or two beforehand, and it was fitting for the groom and bride to meet ahead of their wedding. However, in recent generations, in which the groom and bride meet frequently after agreeing to marry, this custom expresses the meaning of the Sages' enactment to count shiv'a neki'im ahead of the wedding, and it has therefore gradually been accepted in many communities in Israel. This custom also has a halakhic basis in the view of Tosafot and Rosh cited in the previous note, according to which the concern of desire increases the closer the wedding date approaches, and therefore it is ideally better not to meet, so as not to increase the concern of desire. A further benefit: since in the days before the wedding the yearning increases, it is proper for the groom and bride to set more boundaries for themselves so that they do not stumble. However, since this custom is not obligatory, when there is a need they may meet.
When the groom and bride arrive at the wedding hall, they need not make an effort not to see each other, for since they are about to marry now there is no concern of dam ḥimud, since dam ḥimud stems from a yearning that cannot be fulfilled, and that is the aspect of lack and impurity in this desire, whereas here they are about to marry in holiness and purity, and therefore there is no concern about their seeing each other.

sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva for the groom and bride to be aroused to teshuva (repentance) ahead of their wedding, and especially on their wedding day, and to pray to God that they merit to live together in love and joy, and merit to engage in Torah and mitzvot, and to help each other realize all their talents and fulfil all their good aspirations, for the glory of the Torah and the building of the nation and the land. And that they merit to honour their parents, and to have children and raise them to Torah, to mitzvot, to the ḥuppa and to good deeds. And that they merit good health and a good livelihood. And that they merit to observe Shabbatot and festivals with joy and contentment. And it is good for them to pray also for their family members and friends.

The Sages said (Yevamot 63b): "Once a man marries a woman, his sins are stopped up (sealed), as it is stated (Mishlei 18:22): 'He who finds a wife finds good, and obtains favour from the Lord.'" The bride too merits this on her wedding day, for everything the Sages said about the groom applies also to the bride. The reason their sins are forgiven is that while they are single they are like two halves that have not found their completion, as the Sages said (Yevamot 63a): "Any man who has no wife is not a man." And they still dwell without joy, without blessing, without goodness, without Torah, without a wall, without peace (ibid. 62b). By marrying in faith and love according to the law of Moshe and Israel, they unite and complete themselves and are like someone born anew, and their sins, which had influenced their character for the worse, are hidden away and stopped up. If they merit to return in complete teshuva, their sins will be transformed into merits, and together with all their good inclinations they will grow and flourish, deepening and enlarging their love and enriching their lives. But if they return to sin, the sins will return to their place, and the bad inclinations and aspects of their character will spring up like thorns and embitter their lives.

On Yom Kippur we make great efforts to return in teshuva sincerely and honestly, whereas on the wedding day, because of the great holiness of the occasion, the groom and bride can merit this without special efforts. For they truly want to live from now on in faith and love, to build a good family and to do good deeds. Therefore their teshuva is accepted on this day in a special way, and consequently their prayers are answered.

sections.title_en: The Custom of Fasting on the Wedding Day
sections.body_en:
In most communities of Israel the custom is that grooms and brides fast on their wedding day, in order to purify and refine themselves through teshuva, and out of this to pray to God that He grant them, in His abundant kindness, to fulfil all their good aspirations. In addition, there was a concern that out of tension and pressure some grooms would eat and drink excessively and would not come to the ḥuppa with the proper seriousness, and perhaps would not even be focused because of drinking alcoholic beverages. There are communities of Sephardic and Eastern origin in which the custom was not to fast on the wedding day, and there are communities in which the custom was that grooms fast and brides do not, and the brides' teshuva was accomplished through their tevila ahead of the wedding. In practice, it is proper for every groom to follow the custom of his father and every bride that of her mother. And ba'alei teshuva (those who have returned to observance) should choose the custom that seems good to them.

Even in families whose custom is to fast, one does not fast on days on which it is forbidden to fast, such as Rosh Ḥodesh, Ḥanukka and the month of Nisan. A groom or bride who fears that the fast will weaken them or give them headaches is not obligated to fast. Admittedly, in the past only a few were lenient in this, but today, after we have grown accustomed to lives of plenty and comfort, fasts have become more difficult emotionally, and therefore when the fast causes distress we are lenient, since this fast is meant to arouse teshuva and not to bring atonement and refinement through accepting suffering. We find the same with regard to other fasts: in the past many used to fast on them for atonement and refinement through accepting suffering, whereas today the accepted guidance is to increase charity, Torah study and teshuva instead of fasting. Therefore, those who are concerned about the fast are not obligated to fast; they should eat and drink as they need, refrain from alcoholic drink, and arouse themselves to teshuva by setting a time for Torah study on the wedding day and by giving charity. And if they are able, it is better that they fast until midday.

The custom of fasting continues until after the ḥuppa or until tzeit ha-kokhavim, whichever comes first (Ḥokhmat Adam 129:2; Sedei Ḥemed, Ma'arekhet Ḥatan Ve-kalla 4).7

notes_en.en:
The custom of fasting for the groom and bride was widespread in all communities of Ashkenazic origin (Responsa Maharam Mintz 109; Rema EH 61:1; OḤ 573:1). Some mistakenly claim that in all the Sephardic and Eastern communities the custom was not to fast, but in truth in most communities the custom was to fast. There are communities in which both the groom and the bride customarily fasted, among them the communities of the Balkans, Kurdistan and Algeria (Knesset Ha-gedola EH 62, Hagahot Ha-Tur 15; Zeh Ha-shulḥan 104:15). There are communities in which only the groom customarily fasted, among them Babylonia and most communities of North Africa, including Morocco, Djerba and Libya (Ben Ish Ḥai, Shoftim 13; Nahagu Ha-am, Ḥatuna 11; Shemesh U-magen vol. 2, EH 21:3; Sho'el Ve-nish'al vol. 3, OḤ 2 and 4; Siddur Od Avinu Ḥai p. 685). The communities in which the custom was not to fast at all: Syria, Egypt, Constantinople, and all the communities of Yemen (Birkei Yosef OḤ 470:2; Mizbaḥ Adama 23b). So too, in recent generations, have some of the immigrants to the Land of Israel from the Sephardic and Eastern communities practised (Yabi'a Omer vol. 3, 8:17; 9). The proper practice is that every groom follow his father and every bride her mother, and when it is hard for them to fast, they should fast until midday.
The groom and bride do not need to formally accept the fast upon themselves at Minḥa before the wedding day, since they are fasting according to the custom accepted in many communities (MB 562:11). Some have the custom not to fast on days on which Taḥanun is not recited either (Eliyahu Rabba 573:3).

sections.body_en:
There is a special virtue in the first union, which is also called be'ilat mitzva (the mitzva union), in which the groom and bride unite in complete union and make an eternal covenant between them. As Adam said after he met his wife and married her: "And the man said: This one at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh" (Bereishit 2:23-24). Through this they will be able to continue to express their unity in the mitzva of ona, in love and joy, all the days of their lives. And through this they will also merit to fulfil the mitzva of peru u-revu (being fruitful and multiplying) (Tosafot Ketubot 4a).

The betulim (virginity) express the bride's guarding of herself for her husband, so that he will open the wellspring of life within her, and out of pleasure and joy she will merit to bear him sons and daughters. In this union that opens the betulim there is pleasure, and sometimes also pain, which expresses the covenant that the groom and bride make between them – a covenant that will endure always, for better and for worse. As it is stated (Yeḥezkel 16:6): "And I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood, and I said to you: In your blood, live; and I said to you: In your blood, live." That is to say, although the world is full of imperfections, and the groom and bride too are not perfect, the bride's readiness to open herself to her groom so that they can unite, and the groom's readiness to commit himself to caring for her happiness, cover over every deficiency. Thereby an eternal covenant is made between them, through whose fulfilment they will merit to continue their shared life forever – in this world through their descendants, and in the World to Come through the union of their souls.8

notes_en.en:
On the question of why the first union is called be'ilat mitzva, Tosafot explained (Ketubot 4a, s.v. "be'ilat mitzva") that through it the man and woman are bound in a covenant, and out of this they will come to the mitzva of peru u-revu. This is what I wrote above. Some understood that be'ilat mitzva is only a preparation for the mitzva of peru u-revu, since the Sages said (Yevamot 34b) that a woman does not conceive from the first intercourse (see Baḥ EH 63:1; Ḥatam Sofer, Ketubot 4a; Torat Ḥayim OḤ 70:5). However, as explained in Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 1:4; 2:1, the mitzva of ona stands on its own and does not depend on the mitzva of peru u-revu, and this is the great mitzva in be'ilat mitzva, in which they begin to fulfil the mitzva of ona (in line with the words of Tosafot), and out of this they will also merit the mitzva of peru u-revu. So too Hit'orerut Teshuva 1:41 explains that it is called be'ilat mitzva even in the case of a barren woman, because through it "she draws close to him, and they come to brotherhood, love, companionship and peace…".
The covenant is made with self-sacrifice: just as brit mila for males, so be'ilat mitzva, with the opening of the betulim, for the bride. And since it was made in blood, it endures even in moments of crisis and covers over the failings, as is stated regarding the Exodus from Egypt (Yeḥezkel 16:6-8): "And I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood, and I said to you: In your blood, live; and I said to you: In your blood, live. I made you a myriad, like the plants of the field, and you increased and grew… And I passed by you and saw you, and behold, your time was the time of love; and I spread My robe over you and covered your nakedness, and I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God, and you became Mine." The Exodus from Egypt is considered the kiddushin (betrothal) between God and His people Israel (Peninei Halakha: Mo'adim 13:2), akin to the breaking of the betulim in be'ilat mitzva. For when Israel went out of Egypt, God gave them two mitzvot involving blood, brit mila and the korban Pesaḥ (Paschal offering) (in which, with self-sacrifice, they offered up the god of Egypt), as it is stated: "And I said to you: In your blood, live; and I said to you: In your blood, live" (Pesikta Rabbati 17).
There were communities in which the custom was that the groom, after finding his bride to be a virgin, would recite a blessing of praise and thanksgiving: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who set a nut in the Garden of Eden, a lily of the valleys; let no stranger rule over the sealed spring; therefore the loving doe has kept herself in purity and has not broken the statute. Blessed are You, Lord, who chooses the seed of Avraham." This blessing is not mentioned in the Talmud, but it is cited in the writings of many Geonim and Rishonim, among them: Rav Amram Gaon; Rosh, Ketubot 1:15; Tur EH 63; and it is cited as a custom in the name of "some say" in SA EH 63:2. Rema added, based on Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, that it must be recited over a cup of wine. However, today it is not customary to recite it (Arukh Ha-shulḥan EH 63:10).

sections.title_en: Virginity in the Past and Today
sections.body_en:
The ketuba that the Sages instituted is meant to secure the bride's rights, and at its centre is the sum she will receive should the marriage come to an end, through divorce or the husband's death. Regarding the amount of the ketuba, the Sages instituted that one who marries a betula (virgin), since he merits to know that he is her only one, obligates himself for at least two hundred zuz, and one who marries a bride who is not a virgin obligates himself for at least one hundred zuz (Ketubot 10b). In the past, if no blood came out after the be'ilat mitzva, it became clear that the bride had not been a virgin, and the groom could claim that since he had married her on the assumption that she was a virgin, the marriage should be annulled, or the sum of the ketuba reduced. But today, when no blood is found after the be'ilat mitzva, it is not possible to make this claim, for since the bride is older, over the age of eighteen, sometimes the hymen naturally stretches by itself and the opening opens, and no blood comes out as a result of the union. The older the bride, the greater the chance that no blood will come out at the first union, and if the bride was also accustomed to using a tampon during her period, most likely the hymen has stretched and she will not see blood.9

Although, as a result of the later age of marriage, the hymen is often already stretched and does not break at the be'ilat mitzva, the virtue of be'ilat mitzva still remains in place, for through it the groom and bride unite and make an eternal covenant.10

notes_en.en: Based on Ketubot 36a-b, according to Rabbeinu Ḥananel and Rif, if the bride is a bogeret (over the age of twelve and a half, who has already seen a veset), it is possible that she no longer has betulim that bleed, and therefore the groom's claim is not accepted if he claims that since no hymenal blood came out of her, this is a sign that she had been unchaste, and he therefore wishes to divorce her without paying her ketuba. According to Rashi, Rambam, Ramban and Re'ah, his claim is a valid claim, and he can divorce her without paying her ketuba. This is also the ruling of SA EH 68:3. However, they too agree that if the bride has reached around the age of eighteen, he can no longer claim that since no blood came out of her it is a sign that she had been unchaste, since at the age of eighteen there are virgins whose hymen has stretched and who do not bleed. As the years pass the likelihood of this increases, especially when the virgin uses a tampon, which stretches the hymen (Rosh Aryeh 20; Rav Yo'ezer Ariel, Assia vol. 11. See Zikhron Ya'akov 25; Brit Kehuna vol. 2, 9:5).

One may say that when girls used to marry close to the age of twelve, the readiness of the young brides to give themselves over to the pain of the tearing of the hymen expressed the making of the covenant. However, on the other hand, the agreement to marry was easy, since society and family paved the young girl's way to marriage without her needing to deliberate over it. In contrast, in recent generations the age of marriage has risen beyond eighteen, and consequently the responsibility of choice placed upon the bride has intensified: she must decide to give up all the other proposals she might receive in the future, to make an eternal covenant with the one her heart has chosen, and to pray to God that He help them build their home in love and joy, and have children and raise and educate them properly. Similarly, the responsibility placed upon the groom in our day has also intensified, for since grooms are older they cannot rely on their parents' judgment as in the past, and the groom must decide to give up all the other proposals he might receive in the future, to make an eternal covenant with his bride, and to commit himself to stand by her always with faithfulness and love. Therefore, although the matter of the opening of the betulim has diminished, the virtue of be'ilat mitzva remains in place, for it expresses their choice to make an eternal covenant and to unite completely.

sections.body_en:
The Sages instituted that after the groom is secluded with his virgin bride and they have performed the be'ilat mitzva completely, the bride becomes impure on account of the dam betulim. But the groom need not hurry to withdraw after his seed has come out; rather, they are permitted to continue embracing in the position of union. When they decide to part, the groom withdraws from the bride and they begin to observe all the harḥakot of the days of nidda.

Admittedly, by Torah law dam betulim is considered dam makka, that is, blood of a wound, which does not render impure. However, the Sages were concerned that out of the excitement of the breaking of the hymen, blood that does render impure might come out of the uterus together with the hymenal blood. It seems that the Sages were also concerned that if they were lenient about dam betulim, the hymenal bleeding might continue in the subsequent unions as well, since these take place in succession without time for the wound to heal, and then, even when the veset begins, there would be those who would mistakenly think it is dam betulim and would transgress a prohibition punishable by karet. This is especially so in the days after the wedding, when the desire of the groom and bride intensifies, and if they do not make a safeguard and treat all blood as forbidden, they may come to a prohibition.11

Even if after the union the bride did not see dam betulim, they must separate as with a nidda, for since she was a virgin, perhaps a little blood came out of her and was lost, or semen covered it. This is on condition that both of them are sure that there was a complete union, in such a way that the entire organ entered the vagina and the seed came out. But if they are in doubt about this: if they saw blood on the sheet or on the cloth with which they wiped themselves, she has become impure, and if they did not see blood, she is pure. Only after they have had a complete union does she become impure even if they did not see blood, lest blood came out and they did not see it. To avoid the doubt, it is preferable that they use a dark sheet and cloths on which blood is not seen, and then, if they are in doubt whether there was a complete union, they will not need to separate.12

A bride who is not a virgin, such as a widow or a divorcee, or even a single woman who has already had marital relations not in holiness, does not become impure at the first union, since she has no dam betulim.

notes_en.en:
The conclusion of the Gemara in Nidda 65b is that dam betulim renders her forbidden, and therefore: "He performs the be'ilat mitzva and withdraws." The Geonim explained that dam betulim was forbidden lest the breaking of the hymen stimulate bleeding from the uterus, and so wrote Rid, Riaz and Rashba. It is implied by Rav Hai Gaon that this is the usual occurrence, as cited in the Yerushalmi (Berakhot 2:6), that there cannot be dam betulim without menstrual blood. Some say that the Sages were also concerned that out of desire at the first intercourse she might see dam ḥimud (Eshkol). Rosh (Nidda 10:1) further wrote that they wished to make the laws uniform, "because be'ilat mitzva is entrusted to all, and not everyone is expert in distinguishing… between whether she saw or did not see. And also because a groom's inclination overpowers him…". That is, they were concerned that out of the leniency regarding dam betulim they would continue to be lenient even when she sees forbidden blood, as explained above. Even a woman whose bleeding has stopped (mesuleket damim), for example one who takes hormonal pills to postpone the veset, becomes impure from dam betulim.
The be'ilat mitzva is performed in its normal manner, without restriction (Ramban, Rashba, Rosh, Razah, Semag, Sefer Ha-teruma, unlike Ra'avad). This implies that they may continue embracing each other in the position of union until they decide to part, and from when they part they begin the prohibitions of harḥakot. (On this basis some are lenient to wait for a further erection, since as long as they have not parted they have not become forbidden; see Shevet Ha-Levi 5:121.)

The Rishonim disagree whether a bride who did not see blood has become impure. According to Ra'avad, Sefer Ha-teruma and Kol Bo, she is pure, since even when blood came out she is impure only because of the concern that impure blood came out following the dam betulim, and when no blood came out there is no concern. Most Rishonim ruled that she is impure, because perhaps blood came out and was lost or was covered by semen (Ramban, Rashba, Rosh, Mordekhai, Tur and SA YD 193:1). However, one must be stringent in this only on condition that there was gemar bi'a (completed intercourse), that is, a complete union in which the entire organ entered the vagina in a state of erection and his seed came out inside her. But otherwise, if she did not see blood, she is pure (Rema 193:1; Sidrei Tahara 193:3; Ḥokhmat Adam 115:15; Ben Ish Ḥai, Tzav 19). Admittedly, some hold that if, in addition to their doubt whether there was gemar bi'a, the bride felt pain, one should be stringent (Badei Ha-shulḥan 193:19; see Mishmeret Ha-tahara 193:11), but in practice, if the groom or bride is in doubt whether there was gemar bi'a, then even though the bride felt pain, as long as she did not see blood she is pure. For one should not be stringent in a situation of doubt regarding a law whose basis is rabbinic (dam betulim) and which is disputed (since Ra'avad and those who agree with him are lenient). This is especially so in our day, when there is often no dam betulim, since brides are mature, aged eighteen and older, and many use a tampon during their period. In addition, experience shows that the groom and bride often think there was gemar bi'a, and after they separated and she immersed and they again fulfilled the mitzva, they realized they had been mistaken. Feeling pain, too, does not indicate that the hymen was broken, as experience shows.
Therefore, if the groom or bride was in doubt whether there was gemar bi'a, they should check the sheet and the cloths with which they wiped themselves: if there was blood, she is impure, and if there was no blood, she is pure. Better still, they should spread a dark sheet from the outset and use dark cloths on which blood is not seen, and then, if there was a complete union, they separate, and if not, in any event they do not separate, since they cannot see blood there. It is proper to instruct grooms and brides that when they intend to perform the be'ilat mitzva, in order to prevent pain, they should ensure that there is ample moisture in the vagina, and if necessary use lubricants, and then perform the be'ilat mitzva in a single motion, so that doubts do not arise as a result of incomplete intercourse. In addition, in this way the pain generally lessens.

sections.title_en: The Bride's Purification After Dam Betulim
sections.body_en:
After the groom and bride separate from each other, she cannot immediately begin counting shiv'a neki'im, since we learned (above, 4:5-7) that as long as semen may come out of the vagina, a woman cannot begin to become pure. And since for three full days the semen may still come out, she should wait until the fourth day from the union and toward its end perform the hefsek tahara, and then begin the shiv'a neki'im. If she wishes, on the day after the union she may thoroughly wipe the vagina to clean it of all remnants of semen, and on that same day, before sunset, perform the hefsek tahara and begin counting shiv'a neki'im.13

In practice, however, the widespread custom is that the bride takes pills to postpone the veset, and immediately after the complete union she stops taking them, and within a few days she gets her veset, and then only after the veset blood ends can she perform the hefsek tahara and begin counting shiv'a neki'im.

If, after the bride has become pure and they have had union, she again sees blood from her hymen, she becomes impure again, and so too a third time, for as long as remnants of her hymen remain and she sees blood from them, she becomes impure. The distress this causes is very great; therefore everything should be done to prevent repeated impurity from dam betulim. The advice for this is that on the day after the be'ilat mitzva in which the bride became impure from dam betulim, she should feel the area of the hymen with a damp cloth in order to remove the remnants of the hymen (as explained in the note). Experience shows that after this procedure the chance that she will see blood again is very low. Then, if she nevertheless sees blood on days on which she is not expected to get her veset, this blood will no longer be considered dam betulim, which renders impure, but rather blood that came out of a wound formed on the sides of the vagina as a result of the removal of the hymen, which does not render impure.14

notes_en.en: It is explained above (ch. 4, n. 7) that SA and Rema disagree about the law of a woman who emits semen. However, regarding dam betulim, even according to the custom of Rema one waits four days and not five. In addition, regarding dam betulim, some Ashkenazic poskim were lenient to rely on cleaning the vagina, in accordance with the view of SA, so that she may perform the hefsek tahara on that very day, as explained above. This is the view of Rav Rabinovitch and Rav Lior, as cited in the book PUAH vol. 1, ch. 7, n. 46. It is likewise explained above (ch. 4, n. 7) that some Ashkenazic poskim were lenient regarding a ketem, and it seems that they too would be lenient regarding dam betulim. I have already explained there (4:7) that whenever there is an additional reason to be lenient in accordance with the view of SA, one may rely on it.

Guidance for removing the remnants of the hymen: on the day after the be'ilat mitzva, wrap a finger in a wet cloth, insert it into the vagina, and turn it in all directions several times. Afterwards wrap two fingers and repeat the same action. She should do this even if it is somewhat painful, until she feels that nothing remains obstructing the vagina. The bedika of hefsek tahara and the bedikot of the shiv'a neki'im should be performed gently, so as not to injure the sensitive area. If despite this she sees blood on the ed bedika, as long as it is clear that it is from the wound, it does not render impure. According to the experience of my wife, the Rabbanit, brides who did this did not see blood afterwards. In any event, if she sees blood after union, it should be regarded as dam makka, that is, blood of a wound, which does not render impure. There are cases in which the hymen is strong and the bride does not succeed in doing this, and then the advice is to go to a doctor who will remove it, as explained in the next section.
When the bride did not remove the remnants of the hymen, and after the second union they found blood on the sheet or on the wiping cloth, she has become impure. So too the third and fourth time, and so on. However, some say there is no obligation to check the sheet and the wiping cloth, but if they saw blood on them she has become impure; and some say that if she felt pain it is proper to check (see Arukh Ha-shulḥan 193:11; Sho'el Ve-nish'al 2:99; Darkhei Tahara 10:34, in the note; Taharat Ha-bayit 10:6). Some suggest that from the outset they wipe themselves with dark coloured cloths, so that if the blood is slight it will not be seen. But this advice is less good, since a lot of blood may still come out, which would be seen even on a coloured cloth or coloured underwear. Therefore it is proper to make use of the suggestion to remove the remnants of the hymen.

sections.title_en: Removing the Hymen by a Medical Procedure
sections.body_en:
When union is too painful, and after several attempts the groom and bride realize that they are not succeeding in breaking the hymen, because it is particularly thick or because they are particularly apprehensive, they should go to a doctor who will open the hymen with a minor surgical procedure. According to halakha, even though blood comes out from this procedure, the bride does not become impure. For the Sages' enactment is that the bride becomes impure from dam betulim that came out during union, lest, out of the arousal that accompanies union with the groom, veset blood or dam ḥimud also come out of her uterus; but when the hymen was opened by a medical procedure there is no such concern. Afterwards, even if the bride sees blood following union, it will be dam makka, which does not render impure, since it came out from the wound left in the vagina and not from the hymen itself.

Likewise, a woman who did not succeed in carrying out the advice mentioned in the previous section may go to a doctor who will check whether her hymen has opened completely, and if the doctor sees that part of it still obstructs the opening, she will open what remains. Then, if the next time the bride sees blood after union, this blood will be considered blood of a wound, and she will not become impure from it.15

notes_en.en: According to Tzitz Eliezer 10:25:12 and Minḥat Yitzḥak 4:58, even when a doctor removed the hymen, the blood that came out renders impure. In contrast, according to Igrot Moshe YD 1:87, Taharat Ha-bayit 10:9, and Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Nishmat Avraham 193:2, dam betulim that came out through a doctor, without union, does not render impure. Since this is a rabbinic law and the reasoning of the stringent opinions is difficult, one should be lenient. When a doctor removed the hymen and blood came down at the subsequent union, according to Igrot Moshe and Taharat Ha-bayit she is impure. However, it seems that the reason one can become impure from the hymen several times is that as long as she does not know that the hymen has come away, the blood that comes out from there has the presumptive status of dam betulim, that is, blood from the membrane that still closes the opening to some extent. But if a doctor removed the hymen in such a way that the opening is completely open, and afterwards blood comes down, as long as it is not the time of her veset and there is no concern that it is veset blood, it should be attributed to wound blood from the walls of the vagina and not to the hymen. And although one could argue that perhaps remnants of the hymen still remain and the blood came from them, since this is a rabbinic doubt – for perhaps nothing remains of the hymen and the blood came from a wound in the wall of the vagina – one should be lenient. In any case, since a medical procedure was performed to remove the hymen, presumably no blood will come out, and consequently they may wipe themselves with a dark cloth, so that even if blood comes out they will not see it, and in such a case perhaps everyone would agree that one may be lenient.

sections.title_en: When the Prohibition of Yiḥud Applies
sections.body_en:
As a rule, a man and a woman who are forbidden to each other may not be alone in a place where they cannot be seen, lest they come to sin. This prohibition is called the prohibition of yiḥud. Seemingly, a husband and his wife during her nidda period should also be forbidden to be alone in their home, but since they have already merited to rejoice together in the mitzva of ona, and will again merit to fulfil the mitzva of ona after she becomes pure, they have the strength to overcome their inclination and wait until she becomes pure. We have already learned (above, 3:1) that the Talmud relates (Sanhedrin 37a) that a Christian priest asked Rav Kahana: You say that a man is permitted to be in a closed house with his wife when she is a nidda – "is it possible for fire to be in flax and not singe it?!" Can young people overcome their inclination and not sin?! He answered him: "The Torah testified about us, 'hedged about with roses' – that even with a hedge (a fence and boundary) of roses, they will not breach it." That is, the safeguards of distancing that the Sages instituted, which are like a soft fence of roses, keep the couple from sin. And this is on condition that they have already had union once.

But if there was a ḥuppat nidda, or if the wife saw a veset and became impure before they managed to have union, they are forbidden in yiḥud until she immerses and becomes pure and they have union.

Even if they lay together in kiruv basar (skin-to-skin contact) without any barrier between them, not even underwear, the prohibition of yiḥud no longer applies to them. But if out of excessive apprehension one of the spouses shied away from skin-to-skin contact without any barrier, and the bride saw a veset, they are forbidden in yiḥud.16

The convenient advice for a groom and bride who are forbidden in yiḥud is that after the wedding they go to the home of the groom's or the bride's parents and live with them until the night of the tevila. During that time the groom and bride should sleep in two separate rooms between which one cannot pass without going through the hallway in which the parents or other members of the household walk (see Ketubot 4a; SA YD 192:4). And when they are not sleeping, they should be careful not to be alone in a closed room; during the day the main thing to be careful about is that the room not be locked, so that the members of the household can enter at any moment. In the evening they must be more careful, that the door be open and the room lit. If the groom and bride want to be in their own home, the way to prevent yiḥud is for them to host in their home two children from their family aged about six or over, so that at night the groom sleeps with the boy in one room and the bride with the girl in another room.

notes_en.en:
Rema 192:4 wrote: "Some say: If she was pure when he married her and he did not have relations with her, and afterwards she became a nidda, she no longer requires guarding." His source is Terumat Ha-deshen 1:253. That is, if they spent one night in purity, even if they were not in skin-to-skin contact, since they could already have had union, the prohibition of yiḥud no longer applies to them. This is also the view of Levush, Shakh (Nekudot Ha-kesef 2), Tiferet Le-Moshe, Pleti, Ḥokhmat Adam 115:9, Leḥem Ve-simla, Sha'arei De'ah and others. In contrast, many disagree with Rema and are stringent. Some hold that only after complete union is there no prohibition of yiḥud (Yam Shel Shlomo, Ketubot 1:6; Maharsham, and others). Some disagreed with Rema but did not write explicitly that complete union is required (Taz 7; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 17, and others), and some inferred from them that even after ha'ara'a (initial penetration) there is no prohibition of yiḥud (Ḥut Shani 192:2:8). And some inferred from them that even after skin-to-skin contact alone, without a barrier, there is no longer a prohibition of yiḥud (Tzitz Eliezer 8:27-28; Ḥeshev Ha-efod 2:146).
In practice, if they lay in skin-to-skin contact and the groom's seed came out during neshikat shamash, that is, light contact at that place, or even during general skin-to-skin contact, there is no longer a prohibition of yiḥud. The same law applies if they lay in skin-to-skin contact without a barrier and the groom did not have an erection, even though his seed did not come out. So it is according to Rema and those who agree with him, and so too according to some of the stringent poskim. In contrast, if one of the spouses, out of excessive apprehension, shied away from closeness, even Rema and those who agree with him would agree that they are forbidden in yiḥud, since their whole leniency applies to a situation in which they could have had union, and no psychological barrier stood between them causing them to be unable even to lie together in skin-to-skin contact without any barrier. And there are intermediate situations, in which they did not lie together in skin-to-skin contact because they were very tired from the wedding; in such a situation Rema and those who agree with him are lenient, and in a pressing situation one may rely on them, since the prohibition of yiḥud for a groom and bride is rabbinic (see Taharat Ha-bayit 9:9).

sections.body_en:
As is the way of the world, grooms and brides want to rejoice together with the joy of a mitzva throughout the seven days of celebration, and are very distressed that the bride becomes impure immediately after the first night because of dam betulim. In addition, many find it difficult to move from a stage in which touching is forbidden to fulfilling the mitzva in the proper manner, which may cause the first union to involve unpleasantness. And if they do not have the chance to get to know each other and give each other joy, the memory of the first days after the wedding, which are supposed to be especially joyful, may be a sad one. In addition, if the bride does not have the chance to experience pleasure, and only a painful experience remains with her from the first union, there is a concern that she will find it hard to free herself from the negative memory and open herself to fulfilling the mitzva of ona with joy.

Therefore, the proper advice is to postpone the be'ilat mitzva to the end of the seven days of celebration, and in the meantime they should give each other joy with great love. And since by nature, when the groom and bride give each other joy, it is very difficult for the groom to restrain himself from emitting his seed, when the groom feels his desire intensifying they should have union by light contact of the organ at the area of the opening of the vagina, in such a way that his seed goes out toward her without the slightest pressure on the hymen.

Some say, however, that it is preferable to hasten and perform the be'ilat mitzva as soon as possible, even though immediately afterwards the bride becomes impure and the couple must separate from each other. In their view, postponing the complete union even involves certain concerns, as cited in the note. Many follow their practice. However, it seems from experience that the correct guidance for our day is to postpone the be'ilat mitzva so that the groom and bride increase the joy of their love.17

notes_en.en:
By Torah law dam betulim does not render impure, and consequently the bride would be pure until she got her veset. Even by rabbinic law, when the bride was a na'ara who had not yet seen a veset, they had to separate only after four days, and if she had already seen a veset, after one night (Nidda 64b, according to Beit Hillel). In many communities in the East and North Africa the custom was to hasten the be'ilat mitzva, since the families of the groom and bride were tense as to whether dam betulim would be found on the sheet, for if not, the groom's side might cancel the marriage (see Rav Pe'alim vol. 1, EH 2). In Ashkenaz it was not accepted for representatives of the families to ask to see the dam betulim (perhaps because the average age of marriage was somewhat later, and consequently there was naturally sometimes no dam betulim), and the custom was to postpone the be'ilat mitzva by a day or by several days. However, Shakh (192:11) wrote that the custom of postponement is a foolish custom and involves concerns of prohibition. So too wrote Ḥokhmat Adam 115:9. There are three arguments for those who hold that the be'ilat mitzva should not be postponed: 1) One should hasten to perform the union that completes the marriage. 2) Lest they perform a partial union that causes blood to come out and they disregard the blood that came out; this is how several Aḥaronim explained Rema 193:1, who wrote that "a ba'al nefesh (a spiritually sensitive person) should take care not to 'play with the young ones,'" lest blood come out and they not see it (Pleti, Pardes Rimonim, Pitḥa Zuta). 3) According to Shelah, when seed comes out not during union, this involves hotza'at zera le-vatala (wasteful emission of seed), and it is difficult to postpone the be'ilat mitzva in such a way that the seed does not come out. So too wrote Maḥatzit Ha-shekel.
However, Responsa Maharam of Lublin 53 implies that there is no problem in postponing the be'ilat mitzva, and he therefore permitted a bride who married on Friday to immerse on Friday night, even though the permission to immerse on Shabbat is for the sake of a mitzva, whereas according to the accepted custom in Ashkenaz they were accustomed to postpone the be'ilat mitzva until Saturday night. This is because the essence of the mitzva of the rejoicing of groom and bride "depends on the bride being pure, for even without intercourse, the groom's rejoicing with the bride is a mitzva… for not intercourse alone is a mitzva; rather, every kind of closeness with which a man gladdens his wife is a mitzva, for every kind of closeness is a joy for her…". Some explained that the Ashkenazic custom was meant to dispel embarrassment gradually, so that they could perform the union properly (see Hafla'ah 192:4; Taz OḤ 280:2; Yad Efrayim ad loc.). And see the article by Rav Yitzḥak Avi Rons in Teḥumin 36, who expanded on the explanation of the Ashkenazic custom and its merits.
It seems that the concern that dam betulim will come out arises when a partial union is performed, but if the groom and bride are careful that there be not the slightest pressure on the hymen, there is no reason to be concerned that dam betulim, which renders impure by rabbinic law, will come out. As for the concern of wasteful emission of seed, even when the seed comes out through embracing (derekh evarim, "by way of the limbs"), according to many poskim it is not considered wasteful emission of seed (as explained in Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 2:18, and in the Harḥavot there, 1-8). And there is room to say that when the seed comes out around the opening of the vagina, even most of the stringent opinions would agree that there is no prohibition of wasteful emission of seed, since in this manner pregnancy is sometimes even possible. If so, here, where the aim of the groom and bride is to dispel embarrassment and tension and to increase love and the joy of a mitzva, this is desirable le-khatḥila.
Some argue that the be'ilat mitzva should not be postponed, because if she sees blood before they manage to have union, they will be forbidden in yiḥud. However, precisely because of this the custom has an advantage, since in practice many couples who hasten to perform the be'ilat mitzva do not succeed in having a complete union, and there are doctors who estimate that this is even the majority of couples, so that in any case there is no advantage in trying to hasten. Not only that, but as a result of the attempt to hasten, more halakhic questions arise, for since they are hurrying, more often they cannot assess what took place; sometimes they tend to think that there was complete intercourse and that they must separate even though they did not see blood, when in truth they need not separate (above, n. 12), and if there was only a partial union and blood came out, then according to the stringent view they are forbidden in yiḥud (above, n. 14, although in practice one should be lenient, as explained there). In addition, often even when they want to hasten to fulfil the mitzva, in practice the be'ilat mitzva is delayed because of fears and tension, and the hastening to perform the union may cause the groom tension that leads to impotence lasting days and weeks. So in practice, the attempt to hasten sometimes causes the be'ilat mitzva to be delayed by more days than under this suggestion, which dispels the fears.
The main point is that according to this suggestion they will increase love and joy, peace and companionship, and the be'ilat mitzva too will be performed with greater joy. In the early years I instructed grooms that ideally they should hasten to perform the be'ilat mitzva on the first night, and that if they wished they could postpone the be'ilat mitzva according to the advice mentioned. Later I added that if their intention is for the sake of Heaven, that is, to gladden their bride, then the choice to postpone the be'ilat mitzva is also le-khatḥila. However, my wife the Rabbanit, out of her experience of studying with many brides before and after the wedding, repeatedly argued that everyone should be instructed from the outset to postpone the be'ilat mitzva until toward the end of the seven days, because otherwise far too many couples are left with a bad experience of the great mitzva of the first union, and this must not be. Over time I came to see that she is right, and this is what I wrote above.

sections.body_en: It is permitted to perform the be'ilat mitzva on Shabbat. It is not to be forbidden on the grounds that one may not do distressing things on Shabbat, since the joy of the mitzva of union outweighs the distress of the breaking of the hymen. Nor is it to be forbidden because of the prohibition of ḥovel (wounding) on Shabbat, according to which it is forbidden to make a wound that draws blood out of the body, because the hymenal blood is considered as gathered and kept in its place in order to guard her opening, and breaking the hymen is not considered making a wound that causes blood to be drawn out of the body in general. Nor is it considered the melakha of improving something by making an opening, because in truth the state of the hymen is considered the more "improved" one, and breaking the hymen is considered spoiling it, which it is fitting to forgo only because of the great virtue of the union between the spouses (Ketubot 5b-7a; SA OḤ 280:2).

Some say that a bride who does not have a fixed veset must verify that union does not cause her veset to appear. For this purpose, once it is clear that the dam betulim has stopped, during the first three times that they have union the groom and bride should examine themselves. This is how they do it: they prepare clean white cloths for examination; before union the bride examines herself to confirm that she is clean, so that she can be sure that her veset has not begun. After union the groom and bride examine themselves with the cloth, to verify that there is no blood on them as a result of the union. After they have examined themselves three times in this way, they will know with certainty that union does not cause the bride's veset to appear (SA YD 186:2, based on Rif, and many Aḥaronim).

In contrast, some say that there is no need to perform these bedikot, because according to most Rishonim there is no reason to be concerned, without cause, that union will bring on the veset (Rashi, Tosafot, Razah, Ritva and others). In practice too, the concern that union will bring on the veset is negligible. This was the practice in several communities (Shakh 186:1).

In practice, the halakha follows the lenient view, that there is no need to perform additional bedikot after the dam betulim has ended. Those who wish to be scrupulous may follow the stringent view.18

notes_en.en:
As we learned above (ch. 6, n. 1), the Mishna (Nidda 11a) states that a woman must examine herself before union. The Gemara there (11b) explains: "Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: They taught this only with regard to taharot (ritually pure foods), but for her husband she is permitted." That is, when a woman in any case had to examine herself morning and evening for the sake of taharot, they required her to examine herself before union as well, but when she does not examine herself for taharot, she need not examine before union. The same law applies to a woman who does not have a fixed veset. Not only that, but further on (12a), Rav Yehuda responded that it is not proper to examine before union as an act of piety, lest "his heart strike him and he withdraw." Rav Huna likewise responded that for this reason one should also not examine after union. So ruled most Rishonim: Rashi, Tosafot, Razah, Ritva, Semag, Sefer Ha-teruma, Rokeaḥ, Mordekhai in the name of Rashbam, and Ra'avad, and this is also the view of Rif according to Ra'avad's interpretation. So too ruled Shakh 186:1 and Torat Ha-shelamim.
In contrast, some learn from the continuation of the Gemara that the halakha follows Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus, that a woman who does not have a fixed veset must always examine before union and after it. So ruled Rabbeinu Ḥananel, and Rosh took his view into account. So too ruled Rambam. SA cited their view as a second opinion, and some understood that he too holds this way in practice (Torat Ha-shelamim 186:2; Ḥavot Da'at 2).
And some say that the intent of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus is that a woman who does not have a fixed veset must examine herself three times to verify that she does not see blood as a result of relations, and this is the view of Rif (according to many). According to Rashba and those who agree with him, she must examine three times after union, and according to Ramban also before union; so wrote SA 186:2 as the unattributed opinion, and so is the view of Shulḥan Gavoha, Leḥem Ve-simla and many other Aḥaronim up to our day. Some say that external wiping examinations suffice (Sidrei Tahara 184:13; Ḥavot Da'at 186:1), and some say that after union the bride must examine deep inside, in the holes and crevices (Ḥatam Sofer and those who agree with him). And some say that a woman who has a semi-fixed veset, that is, she never sees blood before a certain time, for example twenty-five days from the veset, must perform the three bedikot after twenty-five days, even if this takes several months (Ḥatam Sofer). From all the many poskim who did not write this, it is implied that one need not be particular about it (see Taharat Ha-bayit 3:7). In practice, brides do not establish a semi-fixed veset before the wedding, and consequently it follows that the intent of the poskim is that she examine three times immediately after the dam betulim stops (so too wrote Taharat Bat Yisrael 13:1).
In practice, the halakha follows the lenient view: first, because this is a dispute concerning a rabbinic law. Second, most Rishonim were lenient. Third, this was the practice in several communities, as Shakh wrote and ruled (186:1), and so too in Yemen (Taharat Moshe 8:13) and Baghdad (Zivḥei Tzedek 186:2). Fourth, even according to the stringent opinions it is unclear when the three bedikot must be performed – whether on the days when she is liable to see blood or on any day – so that there is an additional doubt here: if she examines immediately after the tevila, then according to Ḥatam Sofer and those who agree with him she will not have performed the three bedikot, and if she follows Ḥatam Sofer she will not perform the bedikot as early as required according to the other stringent opinions. Fifth, some say that according to the stringent opinions an external examination suffices, and this is an examination that women in any case habitually perform after relieving themselves in the bathroom. So too ruled in practice Rav Gustman (Halikhot Yisrael, Nidda 1:11), Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach (Halikhot Shlomo 2:14) and Rav Rabinovitch. (In Igrot Moshe YD 2:75 he wrote that the law follows Shakh but that it is proper to be stringent; but he said that one should not write in a book that it is obligatory, as cited in Mesoret Moshe vol. 3, p. 217.)
